## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlfleetstack{40}{40}{40}{40}{40}{40}{40}{40}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why must the unit of machine learning systems design become the fleet rather than the model?_

Machine learning at fleet scale is judged by the whole system, and a local improvement can move cost into a layer that its designer did not measure. Faster computation can expose a network bottleneck; larger jobs can lose more work to failure; a service that meets latency targets can still lack evidence required for deployment. The model remains central, but its accuracy and execution speed do not determine whether the complete system delivers useful work. Adding accelerators is therefore a design decision about shared resources and obligations, not simply a purchase of more arithmetic. If communication and recovery consume the saved execution time, the expansion can increase cost without improving progress. If the resulting service cannot preserve availability or account for its effects on users, successful training does not establish readiness for deployment. Single-node reasoning remains necessary because every participant still has local limits, but it cannot settle decisions whose consequences cross machines, teams, and operating boundaries. The engineering responsibility is to connect those consequences before accepting the design. That requires evidence about what improves, what becomes more constrained, and who owns the costs transferred elsewhere. A defensible decision may expand the fleet, change how work is distributed, or postpone release until the operating requirements can be met. In C³ terms, the task is to follow the binding compute, communication, or coordination constraint across layers and keep its displaced costs visible.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Synthesize the six principles into a constraint map for distributed ML systems
- Diagnose a fleet design's binding C³ term using measured execution costs and failure exposure
- Analyze how infrastructure, distributed training, inference, operations, and governance interact across the fleet stack
- Translate security, fairness, privacy, carbon, and reliability obligations into measurable design constraints
- Defend a fleet expansion or model-release decision using fitted scaling-law gains, operational measurements, and governance evidence

:::

## Synthesizing Distributed ML Systems {#sec-conclusion-synthesizing-distributed-ml-systems-bac9}

A faster accelerator can finish its local work sooner yet leave the training job waiting on the same congested collective. Scale creates qualitative change\index{Scale Moment!qualitative change} because the binding constraint can leave the node. It moves into the fabric that carries gradients, into the recovery machinery that restores state after routine failure, into the service contract that decides whether capacity reaches users in time, and into the obligations that decide whether the service may run at all. The book opened on that transition, the scale moment, and on the empirical scaling laws of @sec-vol2-intro-ai-scaling-laws-a043 that keep forcing it. Because each further reduction in loss demands a multiplicative increase in compute, demand for fleet capacity does not settle at the size where the last design worked. Each of the four parts since has answered a share of the question that transition raised by naming a constraint, the measurement that exposes it, and the mechanism that moves it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The scale moment and the qualitative shift to fleet-scale systems are established in @sec-vol2-introduction-scale-moment.
:::

A frontier-model production system\index{Frontier model!fleet infrastructure} can span thousands of accelerators, with fabric links, storage tiers, schedulers, serving replicas, security controls, and governance checks supporting the same workload. Any one layer can bind the entire system. In the storage tier, a slow checkpoint can waste an entire training window. Across the interconnect, a congested fabric can erase scaling gains from added compute. In the serving pool, underprovisioned capacity can turn model quality into user-visible latency, while an unmeasured responsibility constraint can block deployment after the technical system works.

That coupling across the stack is what separates foundational ML engineering\index{DAM taxonomy@D·A·M taxonomy!single-node foundation} from distributed ML engineering\index{Distributed ML engineering!fleet stack shift}. The single-node foundation, organized by the D·A·M lens of data, algorithm, and machine, already couples models, data pipelines, execution, and deployment constraints. Distributed ML engineering extends that reasoning to shared infrastructure, distributed protocols, and governance across a fleet.

The physical substrate\index{Physical substrate!hardware limits}\index{Infrastructure!rates and physical limits} supplies the rates that higher layers inherit. Accelerator topology\index{Accelerator!topology}, data-loading throughput, and network contention constrain how the Distribution band\index{Fleet Stack!Distribution band} partitions, synchronizes, and recovers work. The Serving band\index{Fleet Stack!Serving band} converts that coordinated execution into a service with latency, availability, and cost obligations. The Governance band\index{Fleet Stack!Governance band} determines whether the service remains secure, robust, sustainable, and accountable. Six principles state these inherited constraints as engineering claims, in the order of the book's four parts.

## Six Principles of Distributed ML Systems {#sec-conclusion-six-principles-distributed-ml-systems-746a}

The six engineering practices introduced with the fleet stack describe how a fleet engineer works. The six principles of distributed ML systems\index{Distributed ML!governing principles} describe what the fleet's physical and institutional constraints make true, whatever the practice. Each condenses the part-level principles stated at the opening of its part. Part I's fleet principles condense into the first, Part II's distributed ML principles into the second and third (its universal scaling law instead supplies the demand that this section closes by weighing), Part III's deployment-at-scale principles into the fourth, and Part IV's responsible fleet principles into the fifth and sixth; the paragraphs below cite the part-level principles each one draws on. Each also explains why one of the practices is necessary rather than merely prudent. A fleet that loses training progress to routine interruptions must budget recovery as part of normal operation, which is why treating failure as steady state is a practice. A bottleneck that migrates whenever one term shrinks is why the engineer must expect it to move and measure the layers it moves into.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The six engineering practices, from instrument first to co-design hardware with algorithms, are established with the fleet stack in @sec-vol2-introduction-foundational-concepts.
:::

The Fleet Law, the distributed counterpart of the single-machine iron law\index{Iron law!vs. fleet law}, connects these principles to execution costs\index{Fleet law!distributed step time}\index{Fleet law!C³ taxonomy mapping}. It is the step-time equation of @eq-fleet-law, unchanged:

$$ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\NumberOfDevices} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime $$ {#eq-conclusion-fleet-law}

Infrastructure sets the per-device rates behind $\IronLawComputeTime/\NumberOfDevices$ and the link bandwidths behind $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$. Communication and waiting contribute to $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ and $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$; neither is guaranteed to shrink as $\NumberOfDevices$ rises. Failure lands in the same terms. Checkpoint pauses, detection timeouts, and restarts add to $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$ averaged over the run, asynchronous checkpointing and warm restart move part of that cost into $\OverlappedTime$, and a rollback adds the lost steps back to the work the run must still complete. Serving applies the same accounting discipline to requests, including queueing and routing delay. Responsibility and sustainability add no new term, but they spend the existing ones. Verification work occupies compute, approval gates add coordination that no replica count removes, and every second of step time costs joules at the fleet's average power. Their acceptance also requires evidence that execution time cannot supply, such as subgroup error rates, privacy accounting, and energy measured over a stated boundary.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The term-by-term decomposition of the Fleet Law is developed in @sec-appdx-c3-taxonomy-component-decomposition.
:::

Placed on the fleet stack, the six principles follow its four bands\index{Fleet Stack!layered architecture}\index{Fleet Stack!working discipline} (@fig-fleet-stack-conclusion). The Infrastructure band determines physical capability. The Distribution band partitions execution and so carries both communication and failure recovery, one principle per row, while the Serving band bounds runtime delivery by its contract. The uppermost Governance band carries two principles, and they divide it by obligation rather than strictly by row. Responsibility, placed beside the Assurance row, covers every obligation owed to the people the system affects. That includes the security and robustness of the Assurance row and also the fairness and accountability work that @sec-responsible-ai develops in the band's top row. Sustainability, placed beside that top row, covers the resource obligation alone. The arrow that runs the length of the stack marks the scale moment. It is not a seventh principle; it is the premise on which the volume opened, and crossing it is what turns each of the six from a local concern into a fleet-wide constraint.

::: {#fig-fleet-stack-conclusion fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Fleet Stack Revisited**: The eight rows and four bands of @fig-fleet-stack, now annotated with the six principles, each placed beside the row or band that carries it. The Infrastructure and Serving principles span their whole band; the Distribution and Governance bands each carry one principle per row. The arrow runs the length of the stack because scale changes the behavior of every band." fig-alt="Stack of eight rows in four bands labeled Part I Infrastructure, Part II Distribution, Part III Serving, and Part IV Governance. Numbered principles sit to the right: 1 infrastructure determines capability beside the Infrastructure band, 2 communication can dominate beside Distributed Execution, 3 failure is routine beside Reliability and Control, 4 serving is bounded by its contract beside the Serving band, 5 responsibility constrains design beside Assurance, and 6 sustainability is a first-order cost beside Governance and Sustainability. An upward arrow on the left is labeled scale creates qualitative change."}
![](images/svg/fleet-stack-conclusion.svg){width="100%"}
:::

@Tbl-vol2-principles is therefore a decision map rather than a glossary. Each row links a principle to the question, metric, and practice an engineer uses when diagnosing a fleet-scale design, and to the part and chapters that develop it. The part order is an order of dependency, not a ranking of bottlenecks; the workload and its measurements determine which constraint binds, while the layered tiers in @fig-fleet-stack-conclusion locate the governing architectural band.

| **Principle**                            |       **Core Question**        | **Key Metric**                                     | **Practice It Demands**                        | **Developed In**                                                                                     |
|:-----------------------------------------|:------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Infrastructure determines capability** |       What is possible?        | FLOP/s, memory and bisection bandwidth, rack power | Co-design hardware with algorithms             | Part I: @sec-compute-infrastructure, @sec-network-fabrics, @sec-data-storage                         |
| **Communication can dominate**           |    What is the bottleneck?     | Exposed communication time, scaling efficiency     | Expect bottlenecks to migrate                  | Part II: @sec-distributed-training-systems, @sec-collective-communication                            |

| **Serving is bounded by its contract**   | What reaches the user in time? | p99 latency within the SLO, cost per request       | Reserve headroom for recovery and tail latency | Part III: @sec-performance-engineering, @sec-inference-scale, @sec-edge-intelligence, @sec-ops-scale |

: **Six Principles of Distributed ML Systems**: The qualitative shifts that occur when ML systems move from single machines to distributed production, grouped by the part of the book that develops them. Each principle connects to a governing question, the metric that tests it, the engineering practice it makes necessary, and the chapters where the concept is developed in depth. {#tbl-vol2-principles tbl-colwidths="[20,15,20,17,28]"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-scale-facts
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION SCALE FACTS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Six principles of distributed ML systems.
# │
# │ Goal: Keep local numerical claims tied to executable calculations.
# │ Scope: chapter-anchor — six-principles prose, fallacies, and chapter summary share scale facts.
# │ Show: p99 fan-out tail probability, Llama 3 failure cadence, cluster ratio and
# │       effective training time, straggler drop.
# │ How: Direct probability and rate calculations from the stated assumptions.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import HOURS_PER_DAY, Literature, Models, Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class ConclusionScaleFacts:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tail_servers = 100
    tail_percentile = 0.99
    llama_failures = Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_UnexpectedInterruptions
    llama_days = Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_SnapshotDays
    llama_effective_fraction = Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_EffectiveTrainingTimeFraction
    hours_per_day = HOURS_PER_DAY
    straggler_speed = 0.80
    llama_gpus = Models.Language.Llama3_405B.training_accelerators_ref.magnitude
    ref_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # Archetype A reference cluster
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    tail_hit_probability = 1 - tail_percentile**tail_servers
    llama_hours_per_failure = llama_days * hours_per_day / llama_failures
    straggler_drop = 1 - straggler_speed
    llama_ref_ratio = llama_gpus / ref_gpus  # Llama 3 cluster vs. reference
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(round(tail_hit_probability * 100) == 63, "Tail probability changed")
    check(3.0 < llama_hours_per_failure < 3.2, "Failure cadence changed")
    check(round(straggler_drop * 100) == 20, "Straggler throughput drop changed")
    check(llama_ref_ratio == 16, "Llama 3 cluster ratio changed")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    tail_servers_str = fmt_count(tail_servers, commas=False, label="server")
    tail_percentile_str = fmt_int(tail_percentile * 100, commas=False)
    tail_hit_pct_str = fmt_percent(tail_hit_probability, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    llama_failures_str = fmt_count(llama_failures, commas=False, label="unexpected interruption")
    llama_days_str = fmt_time(llama_days, "day", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    llama_hours_per_failure_str = fmt_time(llama_hours_per_failure, 'hour', precision=1, commas=False, style='word')
    straggler_speed_pct_str = fmt_percent(straggler_speed, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    straggler_drop_pct_str = fmt_percent(straggler_drop, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    llama_gpus_str = fmt_int(llama_gpus, commas=True)
    llama_ref_ratio_str = fmt_int(llama_ref_ratio, commas=False)
    llama_effective_pct_str = fmt_percent(llama_effective_fraction, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

The first principle is that infrastructure determines capability. Physical infrastructure constrains both feasible configurations and attainable rates. Memory capacity and safe power and cooling envelopes limit how much state and active hardware a configuration can support. Cluster-wide bisection bandwidth\index{Bisection bandwidth!scaling ceiling} instead limits how quickly distributed work can exchange data (principle \ref{pri-bisection-bandwidth}); insufficient bandwidth can make a deadline or cost target unattainable without making the computation impossible. Storage sets a further ceiling, because accelerators that the data pipeline cannot feed sit idle regardless of their peak rate (principle \ref{pri-io-wall}). These are the memory, network, and energy walls of the scale moment, measured at the scale of the node, the fabric, and the facility. Partitioning, batch size, and communication scheduling determine how those limits bind, and mastering the fleet requires understanding them from chip-level thermal density\index{Thermal design power!hardware limits} to cluster-wide bisection bandwidth.

The second principle is that communication can become the binding term at scale [@jiang2024megascale; @narayanan2021], with its cost set by the bandwidth-latency trade-off (principle \ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}) inside the Fleet Law's $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ term. Communication intensity, the ratio of bytes crossing the network to local FLOPs, indicates network demand relative to arithmetic. Whether that demand dominates also depends on achieved compute and network rates, message sizes, topology, and overlap. Gradient synchronization\index{Gradient synchronization!communication bottleneck} and straggler effects\index{Straggler!barrier latency} must therefore be measured on the synchronous step's critical path rather than inferred from byte volume alone.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The communication-intensity ratio is established in @sec-vol2-introduction-ci-ratio.
:::

Collective communication algorithms, including Ring AllReduce,[^fn-ring-allreduce-collective] popularized for deep learning by Horovod [@sergeev2018horovod], gradient compression, and overlapping computation with communication\index{Communication overlap!collective hiding}, address communication bottlenecks. For dense collective workloads, conventional oversubscribed fabrics often bottleneck, motivating high-bisection fabrics\index{Bisection bandwidth!network fabric} and transport choices matched to ML communication patterns. Recognizing when communication is the active constraint clarifies when algorithmic optimizations will help and when they merely shift work between equally constrained resources, the displacement of overhead (principle \ref{pri-conservation-overhead}) that makes bottlenecks migrate. Expanding the fabric across thousands of nodes also multiplies the components that a job needs at the same instant, and that multiplication makes failure routine.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Ring collectives, communication overlap, and gradient compression are established in @sec-collective-communication.
:::

[^fn-ring-allreduce-collective]: **Ring AllReduce**\index{Ring AllReduce!bandwidth optimality}: A collective that sends $2(\NumberOfDevices-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\NumberOfDevices$ bytes per worker and receives the same amount for message size $\CollectivePayloadSize$, giving $\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx 2(\NumberOfDevices-1)\PermessageLatency + \frac{2(\NumberOfDevices-1)}{\NumberOfDevices}\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}$ under the $\PermessageLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ communication model, with $\LinkBandwidth$ denoting bandwidth in each full-duplex direction. The coefficient approaches 2$\times$ message volume per worker as $\NumberOfDevices$ grows, while remaining bandwidth-optimal for large messages.

The third principle is that failure is routine. A job that needs many components at once can encounter interruptions frequently enough that recovery becomes normal operation. The reliability gap\index{Reliability gap!routine failure} in @sec-vol2-introduction-reliability-gap follows from $(\ComponentAvailability)^\RequiredComponentCount$ under independent, identical component availability and an all-components-required boundary. Meta's experience training Llama 3\index{Llama 3!failure cadence} on `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_gpus_str` GPUs, `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_ref_ratio_str` times the Archetype A reference cluster, documented `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_failures_str` over `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_days_str`, averaging one unexpected interruption every `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_hours_per_failure_str` [@dubey2024llama]. Recovery should automate known failure paths and escalate cases whose safe response requires investigation. A failed rank can stall every other rank in its collective. Under full-job checkpoint recovery, the affected job rolls back to its last checkpoint; other jobs in the fleet need not roll back. For a fixed amount of lost wall-clock progress, wasted accelerator-time grows with the size of the affected job, which is why checkpoint cadence\index{Checkpointing!cadence and recovery} and recovery architecture are first-order design dimensions.

Architects must embed failure handling from the beginning. Checkpointing strategies\index{Checkpointing!overhead trade-off} balance write overhead against expected lost work, and the Young-Daly interval (principle \ref{pri-young-daly}) estimates that balance under its failure and checkpoint-cost assumptions. Elastic training[^fn-elastic-training-membership] supports changing cluster membership, while graceful degradation\index{Graceful degradation!service availability} preserves a defined level of service as capacity diminishes. Each mechanism needs a tested recovery contract; its name alone does not establish that progress or service quality survives a failure. Recovery also needs capacity. A restarted synchronous job makes progress only when the scheduler can again grant it an atomic, topology-feasible gang allocation (principle \ref{pri-feasibility-before-fairness}), which is why fleet orchestration keeps spare capacity, preempts lower-priority work, and admits only allocations a job can actually use. Coordination, the third C³ axis, is not confined to this principle. It is paid in recovery and gang scheduling here, in request routing for serving, and in the approval gates of governance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Checkpoint cadence, mean time between failures (MTBF) analysis, and elastic recovery protocols are established in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability.
:::

[^fn-elastic-training-membership]: **Elastic Training**\index{Elastic Training!dynamic membership}: Frameworks such as TorchElastic respond to membership changes by stopping surviving workers, reforming the worker group, and restarting workers with new ranks. The framework manages rendezvous and membership, while user code remains responsible for checkpoint, batch-size, and learning-rate semantics.

Communication and failure together constitute the operational reality of the Distribution band. Deployment carries both into a setting where the unit of work is a user request rather than a training step, which gives the fourth principle, that serving is bounded by its contract\index{Service contract!useful capacity}. A serving fleet's useful capacity is the work it completes within its latency, availability, and cost targets, not the work its accelerators execute in isolation. Production inference that waits for every worker in a fan-out inherits tail effects [@dean2013], because completion depends on the slowest required response. A request that touches `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_servers_str` has a `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_hit_pct_str` chance that at least one of them responds beyond its `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_percentile_str`th-percentile latency when server delays are independent,[^fn-tail-effect-latency] so a latency that is rare for one server becomes the common case for the request. Routing is where coordination enters the request path. Probing two of $\ReplicaCount$ replicas and sending the request to the less loaded (principle \ref{pri-power-two-choices}) cuts the expected longest queue from $\mathcal{O}(\log \ReplicaCount / \log \log \ReplicaCount)$ under random placement to $\mathcal{O}(\log \log \ReplicaCount)$ in the idealized balls-into-bins model, at the cost of only two probes. On live traffic the gain still depends on arrivals, service times, and how fresh the load estimate is, so it narrows the tail rather than bounding every request's latency.

[^fn-tail-effect-latency]: **Tail Latency**\index{Tail latency!fan-out probability}: The estimate is one minus the probability that every server answers within its own percentile, which under independence is the per-server probability raised to the number of servers; @sec-inference-scale-load-balancing-request-routing-4997 analyzes the tail effects it summarizes. Shared congestion correlates server delays, so a real fleet can sit above or below this figure, and the independence assumption has to be checked against measured traces.

Inside each replica, the memory wall\index{Memory Wall} returns as a serving constraint. Compute (TFLOP/s) can be abundant while memory bandwidth (GB/s) gates small-batch autoregressive decode\index{Decode Bottleneck} (principle \ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}), because weight and KV-cache traffic from high-bandwidth memory (HBM)\index{HBM!decode bandwidth} leaves compute units underused. Batching amortizes weight reads across output tokens, so the binding constraint can shift toward compute, KV traffic, or the latency budget; a replica's execution envelope must therefore be measured before any fleet-level policy is chosen. The contract also has a lifetime. A heavily used model can spend more on inference than it did on training (principle \ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}), so the cost per request, not the one-time training bill, eventually dominates what the model costs to own.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_conclusion_margin_001.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Schematic roofline with a small-batch decode point on the memory-bandwidth slope below the compute ceiling."}

*Small-batch decode can sit left of the roofline ridge.*
:::

Beyond the data center, the contract takes other forms. On a phone-class device the contract is the device's own power, thermal, and foreground-latency envelope, and the device enforces it by admitting background work, including local adaptation, only when the envelope has room. That admission policy has a consequence that reaches back into training. Only devices whose policy accepts the work take part in adaptation, so the serving-side contract also decides whose data the shared model learns from (principle \ref{pri-participation-selects-population}), a bias the fifth principle must then account for. Across a platform of hundreds of models, staged rollouts and per-service reliability budgets enforce the contract release by release, so every release must carry evidence that its targets still hold. Once the fleet can deliver a service, governance determines whether it is allowed to.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ On-device adaptation within phone-class power and thermal envelopes is established in @sec-edge-intelligence-energy-thermal-constraint-analysis-3133.
:::

The fifth principle is that responsibility constrains design. Responsible AI\index{Responsible AI!engineering constraints} translates risk-management frameworks into engineering constraints [@nist2023airmf]. Safety-specific risks such as reward hacking\index{Reward hacking!safety risk}, distribution shift, and scalable oversight show why those constraints need implementation mechanisms [@amodei2016concrete]. Fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and safety are first-class requirements that shape system architecture throughout the ML lifecycle. The part-level principles behind this one span privacy, because released outputs can disclose what a model learned (principle \ref{pri-information-leakage}); robustness, whose evaluation and defenses require mechanism-specific resource budgets (principle \ref{pri-robustness-compute-penalty}); and feedback, because deployed decisions can shape future training observations (principle \ref{pri-sociotechnical-feedback}).

The fairness impossibility result\index{Fairness impossibility theorem} (principle \ref{pri-fairness-impossibility}) shows why some requirements cannot be satisfied by tuning alone. With unequal base rates and imperfect prediction, groupwise score calibration cannot coexist with score balance for both the positive and the negative class, that is, with equal mean scores across groups among people with positive outcomes and, separately, among people with negative outcomes [@kleinberg2016inherent]. It is the score-level counterpart of the decision-level conflict in the admissions example of @sec-responsible-ai, where, under a rule that admits only qualified applicants, equal opportunity and demographic parity could not hold together. The deployment therefore needs justified criteria, evidence that they hold, and an owner authorized to respond when they fail. Monitoring exposes supported disparities but cannot choose the criterion or provide a remedy by itself. These obligations belong in the design alongside performance requirements, which is why the practice this principle demands is to instrument first. Subgroup error rates, privacy accounting, and audit trails must be collected before the decision they are meant to justify, because a disparity that was never measured cannot be detected, attributed, or remedied after deployment. Environmental responsibility extends the Governance band into the physical resource budget.

The sixth principle is sustainability\index{Sustainable infrastructure!first-order cost}. Environmental impact of large-scale ML\index{Sustainable infrastructure!carbon footprint} elevates resource efficiency to a primary engineering constraint [@strubell2019; @patterson2021carbon]. The energy-scale invariant of @sec-introduction-energyscale-invariant-a0d6 supplies the accounting discipline, a fixed boundary for useful work and for the energy it consumes, and the Fleet Law explains why exposed communication and synchronization cost joules as well as seconds, since a step's energy is approximately its average power times $\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)$. The Jevons Paradox of AI\index{Jevons Paradox!rebound effect} adapts Jevons's resource-efficiency argument [@jevons1865coal] to explain why hardware efficiency gains alone do not eliminate power and carbon costs (principle \ref{pri-jevons-paradox}). Cheaper computation can expand deployment, so usage growth can offset per-query savings. An absolute carbon budget\index{Carbon Budget!fleet constraint} bounds emissions only when accounting and admission decisions enforce it over the stated lifecycle and time horizon.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Carbon accounting, energy metrics, and Jevons rebound effects are established in @sec-sustainable-ai.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-sustainability-anchors
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION SUSTAINABILITY ANCHORS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Sixth-principle paragraph on the carbon accounting chain.
# │
# │ Goal: Recall the sustainability chapter's two anchors from the registry.
# │ Scope: paragraph-local — sixth-principle accounting-chain paragraph only.
# │ Show: GPT-3 ≈ 1,287 MWh ≈ 120 US household-years; Poland/Quebec grid
# │       carbon intensity ≈ 41x.
# │ How: training energy / household annual electricity; ratio of grid
# │      intensities (equals the carbon ratio at fixed energy).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Infrastructure, Models, ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.core.units import MWh
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_energy, fmt_int, fmt_multiple

class ConclusionSustainabilityAnchors:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt3_energy = Models.Language.GPT3.training_energy_mwh
    household_energy = ReferenceStats.EnergyAnchors.USHouseholdAnnualElectricity
    quebec_g_kwh = float(Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec.carbon_intensity_g_kwh)
    poland_g_kwh = float(Infrastructure.Grids.Poland.carbon_intensity_g_kwh)
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    household_years = (gpt3_energy / household_energy).to("").magnitude
    grid_ratio = poland_g_kwh / quebec_g_kwh
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(119 <= household_years <= 121, "GPT-3 household-year anchor changed")
    check(40 < grid_ratio < 42, "Poland/Quebec grid ratio changed")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt3_mwh_str = fmt_energy(gpt3_energy, unit=MWh, precision=0, commas=True)
    household_years_str = fmt_int(round(household_years), commas=False)
    grid_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(grid_ratio, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Sustainability thus becomes an engineering discipline with its own accounting chain. IT energy, multiplied by the facility's power usage effectiveness, gives the energy at the meter; multiplied again by the grid's carbon intensity, it gives operational emissions; the embodied carbon of manufacturing the hardware then joins the total. Two links show how far the chain can swing. Training GPT-3 consumed about `{python} ConclusionSustainabilityAnchors.gpt3_mwh_str`, roughly `{python} ConclusionSustainabilityAnchors.household_years_str` US household-years of electricity [@li2020estimating], and the same energy drawn from Poland's coal-heavy grid emits about `{python} ConclusionSustainabilityAnchors.grid_ratio_mult_str` the carbon it would on Quebec's hydroelectric grid. The chain also explains the practice this principle demands. Small efficiency gains compound across every accelerator and every query in the fleet, but the Jevons argument means that usage growth can absorb them, so they bound total emissions only when an absolute budget caps the total; compounding efficiency under a cap, not efficiency alone, is the practice. Energy costs can exceed model development budgets, thermal limits restrict hardware density, and power infrastructure requirements limit deployment locations. Carbon-aware scheduling\index{Carbon-aware scheduling!fleet placement}, lifecycle assessment,[^fn-lifecycle-assessment-sustainability] and efficiency optimization become essential engineering competencies alongside traditional performance metrics.

[^fn-lifecycle-assessment-sustainability]: **Lifecycle Assessment**\index{Lifecycle Assessment}: @Sec-sustainable-ai-hardware-lifecycle-environmental-assessment-66ee evaluates environmental impact across a system's lifespan, including embodied carbon\index{Embodied carbon!hardware lifecycle} from hardware manufacturing. Embodied emissions can become a substantial share of total impact on clean grids or when hardware is lightly utilized.

The six principles describe the qualitative change\index{Scale Moment!production behavior} that scale can produce, and the scaling laws (principle \ref{pri-universal-scaling}) keep carrying a team that pursues lower loss into regimes its previous fleet never exercised. Each new regime brings behavior that emerges\index{Scale Moment!emergent phenomena} from familiar mechanisms, as the scale moment first showed. A training job that scales from 8 GPUs to 8,000 can meet communication bottlenecks, load imbalance, or synchronization overhead that were negligible at 8. Serving shows the same shift in its event rates. At a million requests a day, a one-in-a-million per-request failure is expected about once a day, so an event that never appears in testing becomes a routine operating condition. At that scale, stragglers\index{Straggler!throughput impact} that bottleneck clusters, network partitions\index{Network partition!distributed training} that split training, and heterogeneity across hardware generations\index{Hardware heterogeneity!fleet load balancing} that complicates load balancing become design inputs rather than anomalies.

Scaling laws set the demand for that growth and the Fleet Law (@eq-conclusion-fleet-law) sets its price, so together they say when growth pays and where it breaks. The laws estimate what growth buys; they do not oblige an organization to buy it. Scaling pays while the quality gain a fitted curve predicts justifies what the fleet charges to deliver it, and that charge moves with $\NumberOfDevices$ on several fronts at once. Increasing $\NumberOfDevices$ reduces the ideal compute term $\IronLawComputeTime/\NumberOfDevices$ for fixed work and unchanged per-device rates, while $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ and $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$ depend on the resulting partition and schedule and carry no such guarantee. When independent, identical constant-rate component failures each interrupt the job, the expected interval between interruptions falls as $1/\NumberOfDevices$; correlated failures or different recovery boundaries require a different model. Within a fixed facility, the power and cooling envelope does not grow with the job, and a successful model then pays its serving cost for as long as it runs. Growth therefore breaks on either side of the ledger. On the model side, the breakdown conditions of @tbl-scaling-breakdown mark where extrapolating a fitted quality curve becomes unreliable, for example when model capacity outgrows the available tokens or added data stops supplying new information. On the systems side, the scaling wall\index{Scaling wall!fleet growth} of @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-physics-scaling-amdahls-law-communication-4d7f marks where added communication and coordination consume the compute time that added accelerators save (principle \ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}), and a site's deliverable power caps the configuration regardless of how the work is partitioned. A complete production design has to evaluate both sides together.

## The Complete Production System {#sec-conclusion-complete-production-system-3885}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-expansion
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION EXPANSION EXAMPLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Frontier-model expansion worked example in The Complete Production System.
# │
# │ Goal: Show how doubling the Archetype A reference cluster changes failure exposure.
# │ Scope: chapter-anchor — expansion worked example in The Complete Production System.
# │ Show: 1,024 -> 2,048 GPUs; GPU-only job MTBF ≈ 48.8 h -> 24.4 h; checkpoint overhead ≈ 1.41x.
# │ How: MTBF_job = MTTF_gpu / N; Young-Daly overhead ≈ sqrt(2·delta/MTBF_job), so it grows as sqrt(N).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_multiple, fmt_time

class ConclusionExpansion:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    ref_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # Archetype A reference cluster
    expansion_factor = 2  # scenario: double the reference cluster
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    exp_gpus = ref_gpus * expansion_factor
    ref_job_mtbf_h = gpu_mttf_h / ref_gpus
    exp_job_mtbf_h = gpu_mttf_h / exp_gpus
    # Young-Daly optimum: overhead ≈ sqrt(2·delta/MTBF_job), independent of delta as a ratio
    ckpt_overhead_growth = math.sqrt(ref_job_mtbf_h / exp_job_mtbf_h)
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ref_gpus == 1024, "Reference cluster changed")
    check(abs(ckpt_overhead_growth - math.sqrt(expansion_factor)) < 1e-9, "Young-Daly scaling changed")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    ref_gpus_str = fmt_count(ref_gpus, label="GPU", commas=True)
    exp_gpus_str = fmt_count(exp_gpus, label="GPU", commas=True)
    gpu_mttf_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    ref_job_mtbf_str = fmt_time(ref_job_mtbf_h, "hour", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    exp_job_mtbf_str = fmt_time(exp_job_mtbf_h, "hour", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    ckpt_overhead_growth_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ckpt_overhead_growth, precision=2, commas=False)
```

Consider Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), whose running instance in this book is a GPT-3-class dense transformer trained with mixed precision on a reference cluster of `{python} ConclusionExpansion.ref_gpus_str` and then shipped into a global serving fleet. Checkpoint bursts must land without starving the data loaders, while collective results must arrive before the computations that depend on them. Communication can overlap independent work, but its exposed remainder delays progress. At that scale, recovery planning uses observed write costs and failure rates, with the Young-Daly interval\index{Young-Daly formula!optimal interval}\index{Checkpointing!Young-Daly formula} supplying an approximation where its assumptions hold [@young1974; @daly2006]. Serving service-level objectives (SLOs)\index{SLO!headroom for recovery} require headroom for rollback and fallback, while governance controls\index{Governance!fleet constraints} enforce approved conditions on which data, models, and outputs may reach users. These are coupled rates, budgets, failure exposures, and policy constraints that must be designed before deployment.

The production system begins with physical capacity, but capacity matters only when the rates line up. Physical compute infrastructure supplies accelerators, power, cooling, and fabric; the data tier determines whether data can arrive fast enough; and collective communication determines whether workers can synchronize without turning the network into the bottleneck. These subsystems must be co-designed\index{Hardware-software co-design!storage and communication}: data ingestion must meet accelerator consumption, checkpoint writes must fit the recovery budget, and the fabric must carry the actual collective traffic. These are distinct rates; matching them to workload demand matters more than making their raw bandwidths equal.

Parallelization strategies must fit those physical rates and the expected failure pattern. Data parallelism\index{Data Parallelism!trade-offs}, tensor parallelism\index{Tensor Parallelism!trade-offs}, and pipeline parallelism\index{Pipeline Parallelism!trade-offs} are not interchangeable templates; each changes memory pressure, communication volume, checkpointing behavior, and scheduler complexity. Hybrid strategies\index{Hybrid Parallelism!systems support} become useful only when the surrounding storage, fabric, and recovery design can support the shape of the partition.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ How data, tensor, pipeline, and hybrid partitioning each move memory pressure, communication volume, and the pipeline bubble is established in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-parallelism-strategy-comparison-d92a.
:::

Serving adds a separate acceptance boundary. The contract of the fourth principle judges the model by its latency, availability, and cost on live traffic, whether it runs in a data center replica or on a phone-class device. Some security and robustness controls execute on the request path; others operate during training, release review, or asynchronous monitoring. Each needs an evidence and response path suited to its obligation. Training throughput therefore does not establish that a model will meet live latency, recovery, security, subgroup, and carbon requirements. A fleet expansion raises two linked decisions, whether to accept the larger training job and whether to release the model it produces, and each needs its own evidence.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-expansion-ledger
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION EXPANSION LEDGER (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Frontier-model expansion worked example in The Complete Production System.
# │
# │ Goal: Give the Young-Daly overhead an absolute baseline and turn the
# │       expansion into a stated decision rule.
# │ Scope: paragraph-local — expansion worked example only.
# │ Show: 175B checkpoint ≈ 2.45 TB, write ≈ 24.5 s; overhead ≈ 1.7% at
# │       1,024 GPUs -> ≈ 2.4% at 2,048; break-even step speedup ≈ 1.01x;
# │       accelerator-hours at ideal speedup ≈ +0.7%.
# │ How: overhead ≈ sqrt(2·T_write/MTBF_job), MTBF_job = MTTF_gpu/N (GPU-only);
# │      run time ∝ T_step/(1 − overhead), so doubling shortens the run iff
# │      speedup > (1 − o_ref)/(1 − o_exp); accelerator-hours scale by
# │      (2/speedup)·(1 − o_ref)/(1 − o_exp) ≥ that ratio.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Models, Systems
from mlsysim.core.units import GB, TB, hour, second
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class ConclusionExpansionLedger:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(Models.Language.GPT3.parameters)  # 14 B/param
    write_bw = float(Systems.Reliability.Recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    ref_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # Archetype A reference cluster
    exp_gpus = 2 * ref_gpus  # scenario: double the reference cluster
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    t_write_h = (ckpt_bytes / write_bw).to(hour).magnitude
    overhead_ref = math.sqrt(2 * t_write_h / (gpu_mttf_h / ref_gpus))
    overhead_exp = math.sqrt(2 * t_write_h / (gpu_mttf_h / exp_gpus))
    breakeven_speedup = (1 - overhead_ref) / (1 - overhead_exp)
    ideal_speedup = exp_gpus / ref_gpus  # ideal step speedup equals the GPU ratio
    ideal_accel_hours_extra = (exp_gpus / ref_gpus) / ideal_speedup * breakeven_speedup - 1
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ref_gpus == 1024, "Reference cluster changed")
    check(22 < t_write_h * 3600 < 27, "175B checkpoint write should be ~24.5 s")
    check(0.015 < overhead_ref < 0.018, "Reference overhead should be ~1.7%")
    check(0.022 < overhead_exp < 0.025, "Expanded overhead should be ~2.4%")
    check(1.0 < breakeven_speedup < 1.02, "Break-even speedup should be just above 1")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(ckpt_bytes, unit=TB, precision=2, commas=False)
    t_write_s_str = fmt_time(t_write_h * 3600, "second", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    overhead_ref_pct_str = fmt_percent(overhead_ref, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    overhead_exp_pct_str = fmt_percent(overhead_exp, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    breakeven_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(breakeven_speedup, precision=2, commas=False)
    ideal_accel_hours_extra_pct_str = fmt_percent(ideal_accel_hours_extra, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-expansion-scaling-gain
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION EXPANSION SCALING GAIN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Frontier-model expansion worked example in The Complete Production System.
# │
# │ Goal: Put a number on the benefit side of the expansion ledger, the loss
# │       reduction a fitted compute scaling law predicts for doubling compute.
# │ Scope: paragraph-local — expansion worked example only.
# │ Show: Kaplan compute exponent 0.050; 2^-0.050 ≈ 0.966, a loss reduction
# │       of ≈ 3.4 percent per doubling.
# │ How: L = (C / C_c)^(-alpha_C), so doubling C multiplies L by 2^(-alpha_C).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_math, fmt_percent

class ConclusionScalingGain:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    compute_law = next(e for e in Literature.KaplanScalingLaws.entries if e["axis"] == "compute")
    alpha_compute = compute_law["alpha"]  # published fit, valid only over its studied range
    compute_multiple = 2  # scenario: double the training compute
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    loss_factor = compute_multiple ** (-alpha_compute)
    loss_reduction = 1 - loss_factor
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(alpha_compute - 0.050) < 1e-9, "Kaplan compute exponent changed")
    check(0.03 < loss_reduction < 0.04, "Doubling-compute loss reduction should be ~3.4 percent")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    neg_alpha_compute_math = fmt_math(rf"-{alpha_compute:.3f}")
    loss_factor_math = fmt_math(rf"2^{{-{alpha_compute:.3f}}} \approx {loss_factor:.3f}")
    loss_reduction_pct_str = fmt_percent(loss_reduction, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

For our frontier-model case, suppose a proposed expansion doubles the reference cluster to `{python} ConclusionExpansion.exp_gpus_str` while retaining the fabric and checkpoint tier. Doubling $\NumberOfDevices$ halves the ideal $\IronLawComputeTime/\NumberOfDevices$ term for fixed work at unchanged per-device rates, so the first measurement is whether that saving survives the changes in $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ and $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$ and their overlap. The recovery side can be estimated before any measurement. Assume independent GPU failures at an identical constant rate, with each failure interrupting the job. Counting those failures alone at the registry mean time to failure (MTTF) of `{python} ConclusionExpansion.gpu_mttf_str` per GPU, the job's mean time between interruptions is that MTTF divided by $\NumberOfDevices$, so it falls from `{python} ConclusionExpansion.ref_job_mtbf_str` to `{python} ConclusionExpansion.exp_job_mtbf_str`. Substituting the Young-Daly interval of @eq-ft-young-daly-interval back into the waste it minimizes gives an optimized checkpoint-and-rework overhead of about $\sqrt{2\CheckpointWriteTime/\SystemMtbf}$ as a fraction of wall-clock time. Because $\SystemMtbf$ falls as $1/\NumberOfDevices$, that overhead grows as $\sqrt{\NumberOfDevices}$, and doubling the cluster multiplies it by $\sqrt{2}$, a factor of about `{python} ConclusionExpansion.ckpt_overhead_growth_mult_str`. The model's `{python} ConclusionExpansionLedger.ckpt_tb_str` checkpoint takes about `{python} ConclusionExpansionLedger.t_write_s_str` to write at the registry checkpoint bandwidth, which puts the overhead at about `{python} ConclusionExpansionLedger.overhead_ref_pct_str` of wall-clock time on the reference cluster and about `{python} ConclusionExpansionLedger.overhead_exp_pct_str` on the expanded one. These figures are optimistic. They count GPU failures alone, while switches, network interface cards, and software add interruptions of their own. The full-system analysis in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-interval-failure-analysis-c28d, which includes those failure domains for a cluster about ten times larger, arrives at a correspondingly larger overhead from the same formula. Write contention with data loading or a changed checkpoint size would also require revising them.

The ledger still yields a decision rule. In this example, measured step time covers uninterrupted execution and excludes the checkpoint-and-rework overhead estimated separately. The retained-progress factor accounts for that excluded cost once; a whole-run measurement that already includes it must not receive the factor again. For fixed work, run time is proportional to $\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)/(1 - \text{overhead})$, so the larger cluster shortens the run only when its measured step-time speedup exceeds the ratio of the two retained fractions, one minus the reference overhead divided by one minus the expanded overhead. Here that break-even speedup is about `{python} ConclusionExpansionLedger.breakeven_speedup_mult_str`, so recovery alone does not block the expansion. Short of a superlinear speedup, however, it cannot save accelerator-hours. Accelerator-hours are the GPU count times run time, so doubling the GPUs multiplies them by twice that same ratio divided by the achieved speedup. Even at the ideal 2$\times$ speedup they rise by about `{python} ConclusionExpansionLedger.ideal_accel_hours_extra_pct_str`, and every point of scaling efficiency lost to exposed communication raises them further. The expansion therefore buys calendar time with accelerator-hours and energy, and the communication measurement, not the recovery estimate, sets that price.

That price buys time, not quality, because the work is fixed. Quality enters the ledger only if the doubled cluster spends twice the compute instead of finishing sooner, and there the fitted scaling curve prices the gain. In the compute power law that @kaplan2020scaling fitted (@fig-model-scaling), loss falls as compute raised to the power `{python} ConclusionScalingGain.neg_alpha_compute_math`, so doubling compute multiplies loss by `{python} ConclusionScalingGain.loss_factor_math`, a reduction of about `{python} ConclusionScalingGain.loss_reduction_pct_str`. A frontier run lies beyond the range that fit studied, so the figure shows the shape of the trade rather than this run's gain. Each doubling buys the same fractional reduction, and therefore a smaller absolute one than the doubling before it, while its price, twice the accelerator-hours plus the recovery and communication overhead above, is paid in full every time.

Releasing the resulting model remains a separate decision, because its serving configuration must meet latency targets with recovery headroom and preserve the required security, subgroup, and carbon evidence. A failed gate requires revising the affected partition, placement, capacity allocation, or release plan before proceeding. The decisions share provenance and resource measurements, but each also needs evidence specific to its operating contract.

These constraints can conflict. A communication optimization may increase failure exposure, sustainability requirements may restrict infrastructure choices, and governance controls may consume serving latency or capacity. The displacement of overhead\index{Displacement of overhead!cross-layer trade-offs} requires measuring those transferred costs before accepting a local speedup.

The three workloads introduced as lighthouse archetypes show that no single corner of the C$^3$ taxonomy\index{C³ taxonomy!workload archetypes}\index{C³ taxonomy!binding constraints} dominates. @Tbl-conclusion-archetype-binding-terms follows each of them up the fleet stack. Its first row repeats the representative binding term with which each workload was first characterized; the rows below record what each band of the stack, and the part of the book that develops it, showed about that workload.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The three lighthouse archetypes, and whether each stresses compute, communication, or coordination, are established in @sec-vol2-introduction-archetypes.
:::

| **Fleet Stack Band**          | **Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3)**                                                                                                                                                                                        | **Archetype B (DLRM at Scale)**                                                                                                                       | **Archetype C (Federated MobileNet)**                                                                                                                                                             |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Representative C$^3$ term** | Communication, fleet-wide                                                                                                                                                                                              | Coordination, in routing and placement                                                                                                                | Local compute, within the device envelope                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Infrastructure (Part I)**   | Training state and checkpoints far exceed one accelerator's memory\index{Frontier model!collective communication}, motivating partitioning; frequent tensor-parallel collectives favor the fastest interconnect domain | Multi-terabyte embedding tables\index{DLRM!coordination bottleneck} exceed any device's memory, and live feature lookups demand random-access storage | Phone-class power, memory, and thermal envelopes\index{MobileNet!edge power envelope} cap what local training can attempt                                                                         |
| **Distribution (Part II)**    | 3D parallelism and AllReduce must fit the step budget, and Young-Daly checkpoint cadence tracks interruptions measured in hours                                                                                        | Embedding sharding turns lookups into AllToAll exchanges whose hottest receiver sets completion time                                                  | Federated averaging replaces AllReduce, and over-selection with round deadlines bounds the wait for intermittent clients                                                                          |
| **Serving (Part III)**        | Small-batch decode is bound by memory bandwidth, so batching, KV-cache policy, and lifetime serving cost shape deployment                                                                                              | Feature-parallel sharding and routing must hold tail latency within budget at millions of queries per second                                          | Adaptation runs only in admitted windows that preserve the foreground deadline, and rollouts span weeks of version skew                                                                           |
| **Governance (Part IV)**      | Data provenance, output leakage, and the energy of each training run gate release                                                                                                                                      | Recommendations shape future training data, requiring fairness and drift evidence with accountable response across the serving lifecycle              | Secure aggregation limits visibility of individual updates; differential privacy bounds released information under stated accounting assumptions; participation bias shapes whose data contribute |

: **Archetypes Across the Fleet Stack**: The book's three running workloads traced through the four bands of the fleet stack, one band per part, beneath the representative binding C$^3$ term with which the introduction characterized each. The same Fleet Law applies to all three; the regimes shown here expose different constraints, not permanent bottleneck assignments. {#tbl-conclusion-archetype-binding-terms tbl-colwidths="[16,28,28,28]"}

Read down a column to trace the constraints one workload encounters across the bands; read across a row to compare how a band constrains different workloads. These constraints need not all bind at once. The representative terms describe operating regimes, not permanent assignments of archetypes to C$^3$ terms. Federated MobileNet can be device-compute-bound during local training yet communication- or coordination-bound during a global round with intermittent clients. The same six principles apply to all three; the engineer must measure the workload at the relevant boundary before choosing which term to reduce. Because the binding term must be found rather than assumed, the book's method reduces to a diagnostic procedure, a sequence of steps that is distinct from the principles it applies.

1. Start with the observed symptom, the user-visible or operator-visible failure.
2. Attach the metric that makes the symptom falsifiable.
3. Map the symptom to C$^3$ by identifying whether compute, communication, or coordination binds first.
4. Locate the fleet-stack row that owns the intervention.
5. State the cost that the proposed fix displaces elsewhere.
6. Preserve the audit, safety, security, or responsibility evidence needed to justify the decision.

On the expanded cluster, a training run that falls behind its schedule exercises every step of that procedure. The lag is the symptom. The metric is model FLOPs utilization\index{Model FLOPs Utilization!fleet diagnostic} measured per step, which has dropped since the expansion. A step profile shows accelerators idle at gradient-synchronization barriers, which maps the shortfall to communication rather than to insufficient computation. The owning row is distributed execution, where the collective and its overlap are scheduled. A proposed fix such as gradient compression shrinks the exchanged bytes but displaces cost into convergence and accuracy risk. The evidence to preserve is therefore the convergence and evaluation record showing that the compressed run still reaches its quality target. The same procedure redirects other symptoms. A fairness alert may point to missing labels, insufficient review capacity, or a serving-path threshold policy rather than model weights alone, and a security incident may point to artifact provenance, access permissions, or rollback evidence rather than network perimeter failure. The discipline is to follow the constraint until the row that owns it and the trade-off it carries are visible.

When the fix changes what ships, the evidence from the final step enters the end-to-end evaluation contract\index{Evaluation contract!production release} (principle \ref{pri-evaluation-contract}), one versioned release record that binds the candidate to production-equivalent measurements, accountable acceptance authority, tested recovery, and explicit conditions that invalidate the evidence.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The end-to-end evaluation contract and its versioned release record are established in @sec-ops-scale-end-to-end-evaluation-contract.
:::

## Competencies Mastered {#sec-conclusion-mastered-da67}

The proposed cluster expansion tests competence across the whole stack. Accepting it requires evidence that reduced compute time survives communication and recovery costs, while releasing its model requires a separate serving and governance judgment. Mastery means identifying those dependencies, choosing the measurements that test them, and defending the decision within the stated assumptions. Each band of the stack contributes one checkable part of that defense.

In the Infrastructure band, the governing question is which infrastructure limit binds the workload. An engineer who has mastered this material can match accelerator memory and compute to the model, provision storage and network bandwidth for the required rates, and account for power and cooling\index{Cooling!capacity constraint} as capacity constraints rather than facilities details. In the expansion, that skill decides whether the retained fabric, checkpoint tier, and site power can carry `{python} ConclusionExpansion.exp_gpus_str` at all.

In the Distribution band, the governing question is how to make a workload larger than any single machine behave as one coordinated system. An engineer can analyze communication patterns, select a parallelization strategy, and estimate failure cadence from component MTTF\index{MTTF!failure cadence}, fleet size, and the failure-dependence model. Given a collective's cost model, the engineer can also predict which of its terms grows with $\NumberOfDevices$, as the Ring AllReduce\index{Ring AllReduce!bandwidth scaling} footnote to the second principle showed. In the expansion, this band produced the recovery estimate and the break-even speedup, and it identified exposed communication as the measurement that sets the price.

In the Serving band, the governing question is how a trained model keeps serving value under live traffic. An engineer can budget the serving tax\index{Serving tax!budgeting}, select batching and placement policies, and monitor system performance and input distributions in production so that a working model does not become an inefficient or stale service. In the expansion, this band decides whether the released model meets its latency contract with headroom left for recovery.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The serving tax that distributed execution adds to each request's latency budget is established in @sec-inference-scale-serving-tax-overhead-distribution-5ef3.
:::

In the Governance band, the governing question is who bears the costs and risks of the system's decisions. An engineer can translate security, privacy, fairness, robustness, and sustainability obligations into controls and evidence: access boundaries, privacy budgets\index{Privacy budget!differential privacy}, subgroup evaluations, adversarial, out-of-distribution, and concept-drift tests\index{Out-of-distribution robustness!testing}\index{Concept drift!monitoring}, incident procedures, and resource accounting. In the expansion, this band supplies the security, subgroup, and carbon evidence that the release decision requires. These competencies connect model development to the consequences of deployment. They also supply a test of transfer. When a new workload or substrate appears, the engineer must identify its accounting boundary, constraints, and evidence requirements before accepting an efficiency claim.

## Where the Binding Constraint Moves Next {#sec-conclusion-path-forward-caa2}

The binding constraint will keep moving as workloads and infrastructure change, and the same six principles apply to workloads that are only now emerging. Test-time computation and multi-component workflows move work into the serving path, while new interconnect and packaging substrates change the rates beneath the fleet. Each shift relocates cost without exempting it from the Fleet Law.

### Orchestration and test-time compute {#sec-conclusion-orchestration-testtime-compute-5b1e}

Test-time computation, introduced alongside pretraining and posttraining in @sec-vol2-intro-resourceconstrained-scaling-regimes-062d, moves part of the scaling curve from the training cluster into the serving path, where each additional model step consumes part of the query's latency and resource budget; @sec-inference-logic-wall treated that spending as a per-request budget, the logic wall. The simplest case already changes the accounting. A service that adds a verification call and retries failed answers can improve accepted output quality while increasing latency and energy per completed task.

Composition\index{Compound AI Systems!compositional scaling} extends that pattern into a workflow of several components, often called a compound AI system. Retrieval looks up external information, tools are programs that perform requested actions, and verification checks whether an output meets a stated requirement. A planner, itself driven by model calls, chooses the next action, and a failed check may trigger another attempt. A workflow whose planner decides and acts in such a loop is called agentic. The same fleet constraints govern this larger accounting boundary. Network fabrics constrain communication, memory systems constrain state residency, and governance constrains which actions may execute. These specialized components can expand what the system does, but their contribution must be measured over the complete task and its required quality and safety.

When useful work spans multiple components, the engineer must measure orchestration overhead, state movement, failure propagation, latency budgets, and governance evidence as part of the system itself. The accounting boundary has to grow with the work. That requirement is the measurement contract of @sec-sustainable-ai-part-ii-measurement-assessment-fb0b, a stated functional unit inside a stated system boundary, applied to a workflow instead of a single model (@fig-conclusion-traditional-vs-agentic). For model execution alone, the boundary encloses one forward pass, and FLOPs and joules per token describe its cost. For an agentic workflow\index{Agentic AI!fleet macro-efficiency}, the boundary must enclose planning, retrieval, tool execution, verification, and every retry triggered by a failed check, so the cost is counted in joules per useful task completed\index{Goodput!agentic closed loop}\index{Energy efficiency!joules per useful task}. Conventional serving already requires end-to-end evaluation, but inside such a loop the model calls sit within a control cycle whose throughput and energy hinge on retry frequency and verification latency. Coordination, already paid in recovery and request routing, thus reappears inside the serving path between model calls.

::: {#fig-conclusion-traditional-vs-agentic fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From Model Serving to Closed-Loop Agentic Fleets**: The dashed outline in each panel is the accounting boundary. For model execution (a), the boundary holds only the forward pass, so FLOPs per token and joules per token describe it. For a complete workflow (b), the boundary holds planning, retrieval, tool execution, verification, and every retry after a failed check, with the model called from inside the loop, so the cost is counted per useful task completed. Minimizing that cost requires evaluating the whole loop at the required quality and safety." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel a, model execution: a prompt box feeds a model forward pass box inside a dashed boundary, which emits tokens; the note below reads measured per token, FLOPs per token and joules per token. Panel b, complete workflow: a goal box feeds plan, retrieve, run tool, and verify boxes inside a dashed boundary, with a model calls bar beneath the first three and a red dashed arrow labeled check failed, retry, running from verify back to plan; verify feeds a verified result box outside the boundary; the note below reads measured per task, joules per useful task completed."}
![](images/svg/traditional_vs_agentic_optimization.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Such a loop needs a coordinator of its own. Workflow orchestration\index{Orchestration!layer} schedules model calls, retrieval, tool execution, and verification under latency, cost, and failure budgets, and it is distinct from the fleet orchestration of @sec-fleet-orchestration, which places jobs and replicas on accelerators. The workflow layer relies on that fleet scheduler for resource placement and on production MLOps pipelines\index{MLOps!production lifecycle} for versioning and release, but neither supporting mechanism decides the application's next action.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Cluster scheduling and resource-placement policies are established in @sec-fleet-orchestration.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fleet-evolution-notebook
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FLEET EVOLUTION CALCULATOR (NOTEBOOK)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Fleet-stack efficiency accounting" .callout-notebook
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify where the next 100x efficiency gain must come from.
# │ Scope: notebook-only — values used by the fleet-stack accounting notebook and its lead-in.
# │ Show: orchestration_gain ≈ 10x, hw_gain ≈ 4x, algorithm_gain ≈ 2.5x.
# │ How: Load ReferenceStats.FleetEvolution and solve Target = HW * Algorithm * Orchestration.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_math, fmt_multiple

class FleetEvolution:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    profile = ReferenceStats.FleetEvolution
    target_gain = profile.TargetGain
    hw_gen_gain = profile.HardwareGain
    algo_pruning_gain = profile.AlgorithmGain
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    # Solve for required orchestration gain:
    orch_required = target_gain / (hw_gen_gain * algo_pruning_gain)
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(orch_required == 10.0, f"Orch gain {orch_required} unexpected")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    fe_target_gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(target_gain, precision=0, commas=True)
    fe_hw_gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(hw_gen_gain, precision=0, commas=True)
    fe_algo_gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(algo_pruning_gain, precision=1, commas=True)
    fe_orch_gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(orch_required, precision=0, commas=True)
    fe_known_gains_product_math = fmt_math(rf"({hw_gen_gain:.1f} \times {algo_pruning_gain:.1f})")
```

Measuring the whole loop also changes how an efficiency target is planned, because the retries, duplicate model calls, and repeated retrieval inside the loop become places where efficiency can be gained or lost. A `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_target_gain_mult_str` goal, an illustrative planning target rather than a measured trend, can be split across the stack only if its multiplicative factors hold under the same workload and resource budget. Whatever hardware and algorithms do not supply becomes a required improvement from the two orchestration layers together, not evidence that the improvement is available.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_conclusion_margin_003.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three orange horizontal bars labeled orchestration 10 times, hardware 4 times, and algorithm 2.5 times, longest at the top."}

*In this illustrative split, the residual becomes a requirement on orchestration, not a demonstrated gain.*
:::

:::: {#nbk-conclusion-projecting-100-fleet .callout-notebook title="Fleet-stack efficiency accounting"}

**Problem**: Efficiency here means useful task progress per unit of fleet resource budget, with quality and safety held to the same acceptance criteria. Suppose a workload needs a `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_target_gain_mult_str` efficiency improvement over a large-cluster baseline. If a particular workload saw `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_hw_gain_mult_str` from hardware and `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_algo_gain_mult_str` from algorithmic compression, where would the remaining gain have to come from?

**Math**:
Under the assumed multiplicative accounting, total system gain is the product of compatible improvements across the fleet stack.

1. Hardware (physics): `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_hw_gain_mult_str` in this scenario.
2. Algorithm (math): `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_algo_gain_mult_str` from workload-compatible sparsity or distillation.
3. Orchestration (systems): `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_target_gain_mult_str` / `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_known_gains_product_math` = `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_orch_gain_mult_str`.

**Systems insight**: The division itself is simple arithmetic, and the lessons lie in what it assumes. First, the result is a requirement, not a forecast. Under the assumed hardware and algorithmic gains, the `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_target_gain_mult_str` target leaves a residual `{python} FleetEvolution.fe_orch_gain_mult_str` that orchestration would need to supply, split between the workflow layer (reducing duplicate model calls, routing requests to appropriate components, reusing cached state, validating outputs) and the fleet and runtime layers (placement and overlapping communication with computation). These are candidate interventions, not demonstrated sources of that gain. Second, the factors multiply only when each removes different work. Distillation that shrinks every model call and a routing change that skips some calls compound, but a cache that avoids a repeated retrieval and a planner change that stops issuing that same retrieval save the same work once, not twice. If measurements cannot establish the required improvement within the latency and resource budgets, the target must be revised.

::::

### Physical substrates and emerging hardware {#sec-conclusion-physical-substrates-emerging-hardware-9c47}

Measured orchestration gains still depend on a physical fabric, so software and substrate choices must be evaluated together. Once software has reduced wasted model calls, duplicate retrieval, and avoidable coordination, the remaining frontier is the substrate that moves tokens, activations, and power through the fleet. For Archetype A, the pressure on that substrate comes from specific collective patterns rather than from scale in general. Tensor parallelism\index{Tensor Parallelism!collective communication} issues frequent collectives across partitioned tensors, and mixture-of-experts (MoE)\index{MoE!all-to-all routing} routing issues an all-to-all dispatch at each expert layer. Across thousands of accelerators, link energy accumulates with the volume of that collective traffic, which makes lower-energy interconnects a plausible fabric-efficiency lever.

The candidates are substrates the book has already met.
